doc.title: Carmen Caramanica interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, July 27, 2011

title: Getting the Rawls call and becoming his musical director
summary: Meeting Rawls in New York, Powell taking his number, and the call to join arriving while a local trumpeter doubted him.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Playing in Lionel Hampton's big band

blocks.x: arrogant. And he was always breaking my chops because we said my friend Jack Toker is playing with Lou Rawls and I got a postcard from them and they’re going to be going to Europe. Oh wonderful. And so he would always say things to me like “well gee maybe Lou Rawls is going to call you up to play this gig in Frankfort” or something like that. And I said “well that’d be nice.” And so one time we were rehearsing and the phone rings. And he said “hey answer that it’s probably Lou Rawls.” And it was. And I said oh man, “oh yes, Mr. Rawls, oh thank you, oh call you Lou?” You know, that kind of stuff. And everybody is sitting there and the trumpet player is going “what’s going on?” And he basically offered me the gig. He said “I’d like you to come and play with us, we’re going to be starting and we’re going to Miami for two weeks and then we’re going to go to Los Angeles and we’re going to do this” and he’s telling me his itinerary. “Do you think you could make it?” And I said “oh very much so. Listen, before you go, could you please say hello to a friend of mine?” And I handed him the phone, and this guy just — did one of those kind of numbers. So it was one of those small victories in life that, you know you never believe something like this is going to happen. So I said oh that’s great.
Yeah. And it’s so cool because Lou Rawls, he had such a distinctive voice too? There no like pretending that this is —

So that’s how I luckily got hooked up with Lou Rawls. And then to wrap up the story quickly, because I’ve told this before, after being with Lou for about six months, the musical director who had gotten me into this gig decided he was going to go home to England. And so he suggested me to be the musical director in his place. It’s a little bit on the unheard of side, because basically I had no credentials. I didn’t have a college education, I didn’t have a lot of experience, I mean professional experience, other than being a guitar player on this gig and the duties of a musical director, I know you’re going to ask me that later — it’s a nice list that you gave me because it gives me some time to think about it — you have to write the arrangements for the band. And I wasn’t trained in orchestration. I bought books, I did a correspondence course from Berklee. It was a six month course where they would send you assignments and you sent them back and they’d correct it, and my teacher after two or three lessons stopped sending the stuff back so I just kind of did it on my own. Luckily there were some people around here, the late Chic Esposito was wonderful. I would go to him with my scores and say “Chic, did I do this right?” and he’d say “no, the saxophone doesn’t have that note on his horn” things like that. You know, “check your range.” He would do all kinds of nice tutoring for me. So that was wonderful. And there were other people around that I could talk to that kind of helped me too. But basically it was still by the seat of my pants that I was doing this stuff. © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -7-
